questions.question: The diagram shows how influenza is transmitted. Based on this diagram, which situation would LEAST likely result in transmission of the flu virus from one person to another?
questions.answer: The diagram shows airborne, contact and contaminated object/food routes, but not insect vectors.
options: A fly landing on an infected person, then landing on an uninfected person.
Drinking from an unwashed cup previously used by an infected person.
Being in the same room with someone showing flu symptoms.
Eating food prepared by an infected person.

questions.question: Pasteur boiled broth in swan-necked flasks and broke the neck off one. Why did he use a swan-necked flask?
questions.answer: Air could still enter, but dust and microbes were trapped in the bend.
options: It allowed him to easily observe his results.
The curved neck caught the microbes in air entering the flask and prevented them contaminating the broth.
The glass was easy to sterilise with heat, ensuring better microbial growth.
The curved neck ensured the broth would condense there on boiling, maximising exposure.

questions.question: Newcastle disease (ND) is a highly contagious viral disease of poultry and wild birds; its virulent form can cause up to 100% mortality in flocks and had not previously occurred in Australia. It poses no risk to consumers of poultry products. An outbreak occurs in two commercial flocks in western Sydney, linked to a third flock. Which control measures would most effectively prevent spread to other farms and native birds?
questions.answer: Together these contain movement, remove the reservoir and destroy remaining virus.
options: Destruction of all poultry and restocking with unaffected birds.
Vaccination of poultry farmers and laboratory workers and surveillance of the affected birds.
Quarantine of farmers and laboratory workers and disinfection of the affected properties.
Quarantine, destruction of poultry and disinfection of the affected properties.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

Identify cell X.
questions.answer: A helper T cell.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

Describe the role of plasma cells as shown in the diagram.
questions.answer: Plasma cells, formed from activated B cells, secrete large amounts of antibody specific to the *B. pertussis* antigen. Antibodies bind the antigen, forming antigen–antibody complexes that agglutinate and neutralise bacteria and mark them for destruction by phagocytes.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

Use the diagram and the graph to explain why a child vaccinated against pertussis will not get the disease.
questions.answer:
The vaccine is the initial exposure: it contains the antigen but does not cause disease. B cells with matching receptors are activated with help from helper T cells and form plasma cells and memory B cells. This primary response is slow and produces a relatively small antibody peak.

If the child later meets the bacterium (secondary exposure), memory cells recognise it and rapidly divide into plasma cells. The graph shows antibody production is faster, reaches a much higher concentration and lasts longer. The bacteria are destroyed before they multiply enough to cause symptoms.

questions.question:
Pertussis is caused by the bacterium *Bordetella pertussis*. A vaccine is given to infants. The diagram shows the immune response to an infection.

The graph shows the incidence of pertussis in Australia from 1940 to 2009. Suggest a reason for the trend.
questions.answer: Incidence fell steeply from the 1940s and stayed very low as vaccination became widespread, then rose slowly from about 1990. The rise may reflect lower vaccination coverage or waning immunity (or bacterial changes and better diagnosis).

questions.question: Gumbi Gumbi (*Pittosporum angustifolium*) is an Aboriginal bush medicine for coughs and colds, now sold to non-Indigenous people. Outline what 'bush medicine' means and explain why recognition and protection of Aboriginal cultural and intellectual property is important.
questions.answer:
Bush medicine is the traditional use by Aboriginal peoples of native plants and other natural materials to treat illness, based on knowledge passed down over many generations.

Protection matters because the knowledge belongs to the communities that developed it and is part of their culture. Without recognition, others can patent or commercialise it without consent. Protocols ensure free, informed consent, acknowledgement, a fair share of benefits that supports communities, and culturally appropriate, sustainable use of the plants.

Plot a bar graph of the data.

questions.question:
Lassa fever (West Africa) is caused by Lassa virus. The main reservoir is the rat *Mastomys natalensis*; the virus is in its urine and faeces, and 90–95% of human cases are thought to arise from contaminated food stores. Human-to-human transmission via body fluids also occurs. Weekly confirmed new cases in Nigeria from January 2020:

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New cases | 20 | 69 | 82 | 96 | 102 | 110 | 122 |

Propose a measure to control the disease and explain how it would work.

questions.question:
The graphs show the incidence of skin melanoma and deaths by age for men and women (2009–2013).

Analyse and account for the trends shown.
questions.answer:
**Age:** new cases and deaths are essentially zero in childhood and rise with age, peaking at 80–84 years for new cases (about 165 per 100 000 men, 80 women); deaths are highest at 85+ (about 55 men, 22 women). UV damage to DNA accumulates over a lifetime, and mutations take time to build up in genes controlling cell division; immune surveillance and repair also decline with age.

**Sex:** from about 60 years, men have much higher rates than women (roughly double at the peak), and more deaths. Likely reasons include greater cumulative exposure through outdoor work, less use of sunscreen and protective clothing, and later diagnosis.

**Younger adults:** women have somewhat higher rates than men below about 50 years, possibly due to more deliberate tanning.

Deaths are far fewer than new cases, showing many melanomas are treated successfully.

questions.question:
Australia's SLIP SLOP SLAP sun protection campaign was introduced in the 1980s.

It was primarily aimed at parents. Why do you think this was?
questions.answer: Parents control children's sun protection and habits. UV exposure and sunburn in childhood add to lifetime DNA damage and raise melanoma risk later, so protecting children early gives the greatest benefit and establishes lifelong behaviour.

questions.question:
Australia's SLIP SLOP SLAP sun protection campaign was introduced in the 1980s.

What type of epidemiological study could be used to test the effectiveness of the campaign?
questions.answer: An intervention study (comparing outcomes for those exposed and not exposed to the intervention).

Calculate the prevalence as a percentage of the population.
Describe the cause, effects, treatment/management and means of prevention of a named nutritional disease OR disease caused by environmental exposure. Present the information in a table.
questions.answer:

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Cause | Inhaling asbestos fibres, which lodge in the lungs and cause chronic inflammation |
| Effects | Scarring (fibrosis) of lung tissue, reduced gas exchange, shortness of breath, cough; raised risk of lung cancer; can be fatal |

questions.question:
The diagram shows a process during meiosis involving a homologous pair with alleles A and b on one chromosome and a and B on the other.

Identify the process.
questions.answer: Crossing over.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a process during meiosis involving a homologous pair with alleles A and b on one chromosome and a and B on the other.

Draw the four gametes produced from these chromosomes.
questions.answer: Each gamete has one whole chromosome (chromatid). The exchanged segments carry the lower (B/b) locus, so the four gametes are **Ab** (non-recombinant), **AB** (recombinant), **ab** (recombinant) and **aB** (non-recombinant).

questions.question:
The diagram shows a process during meiosis involving a homologous pair with alleles A and b on one chromosome and a and B on the other.

Explain the benefit of this process to the continuity of the species.
questions.answer: Crossing over swaps segments between maternal and paternal homologues, making new allele combinations on chromosomes. Gametes, and so offspring, are more genetically varied. If the environment changes, some individuals are more likely to have suited combinations, survive and reproduce, so the species persists.

questions.question: Rh positive (dominant) and Rh negative alleles are on chromosome 1. A man is Rh+ Rh+ and a woman Rh+ Rh−. What is the probability that their child is Rh negative? Show working.
questions.answer:
Let R = Rh+ and r = Rh−. Cross RR × Rr:

| | R | r |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | RR | Rr |
| **R** | RR | Rr |

All children have at least one R, so the probability of an Rh negative child (rr) is **0%**.

questions.question: Scientists often study the effects of environment on phenotype using identical twins. Account for the use of this method, with examples.
questions.answer: Identical twins come from one zygote and have the same genotype, so differences in their phenotypes can be attributed mainly to environment. For example, twins with different nutrition may differ in height or body mass; different sun exposure changes skin colour and freckling; different training changes muscle development. Comparing twins separates genetic from environmental effects.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of the structure of DNA, showing base pairing, bonding and the composition of a nucleotide.
questions.answer: Each nucleotide is a phosphate, a deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base. Sugar–phosphate backbones are joined covalently; bases attach to the sugars and pair across the two antiparallel strands by hydrogen bonds (A with T, C with G), twisting into a double helix.

questions.question: Outline the major steps in DNA replication.
questions.answer:
1. Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds, separating the strands.
2. Each strand acts as a template; free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (primase lays an RNA primer first).
3. DNA polymerase joins the new nucleotides in the 5′ to 3′ direction (continuously on the leading strand, in fragments joined by ligase on the lagging strand).
4. DNA polymerase proofreads and corrects errors.
5. Two identical DNA molecules result, each with one old and one new strand, and rewind (semi-conservative).

questions.question: Giraffes range from Sudan through East Africa to southern Africa and vary in colouration and patterning. DNA analysis suggests four species (northern, reticulated, Masai and southern), each with a fairly distinct range (map). Evaluate the effect of mutation, gene flow and genetic drift on the gene pool of giraffe populations.
questions.answer:
**Mutation** is the original source of new alleles (e.g. affecting coat pattern). Only germ-line mutations are inherited. Its effect per generation is small, but over long periods it is essential: mutations accumulating separately in each region make the gene pools diverge.

**Gene flow** moves alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding. It adds variation to a population but makes populations more similar. The four groups occupy largely separate ranges, so gene flow between them has been very limited, which allowed them to diverge and become separate species. Where it occurs within a species, it maintains cohesion.

**Genetic drift** is random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small, isolated populations. Founder events (a few giraffes colonising a new area) or bottlenecks (drought, disease, hunting) can fix or lose alleles by chance, reducing variation and increasing differences between populations. The fragmented patches on the map make drift likely.

**Judgement:** all three significantly shape giraffe gene pools. Mutation supplies the variation; restricted gene flow is what permits divergence; drift (with natural selection in differing environments) accelerates it, particularly in small populations. Drift and lost gene flow also threaten the diversity of small populations today.

questions.question: Thermal pollution (hot or cold water dumped into rivers) harms aquatic organisms. Design an experiment to investigate the effect of water temperature on the growth of aquatic plants.
questions.answer:
**Independent variable:** water temperature (e.g. 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 °C, held by water baths; the normal river temperature is the control).

**Dependent variable:** growth, as change in blotted fresh mass (or stem length) over 3 weeks.

**Controlled:** species, starting size, number of plants per tank, water volume and source, nutrients, pH, light intensity and duration.

**Method:**
1. Set up three tanks at each temperature, each with 10 similar plants of one species.
2. Record initial mass of each plant.
3. Maintain conditions, checking temperature daily.
4. After 3 weeks, re-measure and calculate mean percentage change in mass for each temperature.
5. Graph mean growth against temperature and repeat the experiment to check reliability.

questions.question:
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women. Most cases are linked to infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), a common sexually transmitted virus. Vaccination against HPV types 16 and 18 significantly reduces the risk. Australia began HPV vaccination in 2007 (females) and 2013 (males).

Explain how vaccination against HPV prevents cervical cancer.
questions.answer: The vaccine contains HPV surface proteins (no viral DNA), which trigger an adaptive response producing antibodies and memory cells. On later exposure, antibodies quickly neutralise the virus before it infects cervical cells. Without persistent infection, viral genes cannot disrupt the cells' cell-cycle control (p53 and Rb proteins), so cancer is far less likely to develop.

questions.question:
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women. Most cases are linked to infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), a common sexually transmitted virus. Vaccination against HPV types 16 and 18 significantly reduces the risk. Australia began HPV vaccination in 2007 (females) and 2013 (males).

An infographic shows that smoking also contributes to cervical cancer. Evaluate whether cervical cancer should be classified as an infectious or non-infectious disease.
questions.answer:
An **infectious** disease is caused by a pathogen and can be passed between hosts; a **non-infectious** disease is not transmitted and arises from genetic, environmental or lifestyle factors. Koch's postulates test whether a microbe causes a disease.

**For infectious:** HPV, a transmissible virus, is detected in almost all cervical cancers (types 16 and 18 cause about 70%), and vaccination reduces incidence, strong evidence of cause.

**For non-infectious:** the cancer is uncontrolled division of the person's own mutated cells. The tumour cannot be passed on. Most HPV infections clear without causing cancer, and other factors such as smoking (a source of mutagens; see infographic) raise the risk. Koch's postulates cannot be fully applied, since HPV cannot be grown in pure culture and deliberately infecting people is unethical.

**Judgement:** cervical cancer is best classified as a **non-infectious disease with an infectious cause**: the cancer itself is not communicable, but persistent infection with an infectious agent (HPV) is the necessary cause in nearly all cases, with smoking a cofactor. Prevention therefore targets both infection (vaccination) and cofactors, plus screening.

*Note: the school's sample answer suggests many cases lack HPV; in fact high-risk HPV is found in nearly all cervical cancers.*
